title: The eyes
hook: eyes half open, gaze resting on the floor ahead

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hands: one resting in the other, an oval near the navel, the thumbs as a gauge. Your line: thumbs just touching. Did you check them while you waited? Day one thousand two hundred nine.

A cat lies on a sunny windowsill, eyes narrowed to slits. Asleep? Drop a spoon in the kitchen and the ears turn instantly. Not asleep. Not exactly watching, either. Resting, and still there. Ask people what meditation looks like and they'll often shut their eyes to show you. Zen asks for something else. In a Zen hall the eyes stay partly open, the lids lowered, the gaze down on the floor ahead. A little like that cat. Today: the eyes.
screen: `A CAT WITH EYES IN SLITS.` → `NOT ASLEEP, NOT WATCHING.` → `ZEN KEEPS THE EYES OPEN.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In zazen the eyes are neither shut nor wide. The lids come halfway down, and the gaze drops to rest on the floor a little way ahead, or on the wall in front if you're facing one. It isn't fixed on a spot. It's soft and unfocused, the way eyes rest when someone is listening hard to music. Dogen's guide to sitting is plain about it: keep the eyes open. Second, why not closed. Close the eyes and two things tend to happen. Drowsiness creeps in, the body taking the hint that it's bedtime. Or a private movie starts: plans, memories, imaginary arguments. The room disappears and the mind wanders off into its own theater. Half open keeps a little daylight in. Third, why not wide. Eyes wide open grab. They pick out a crack in the paint, a speck on the floor, the person shifting next to you, and attention follows each one. Lowering the lids takes the grip out of looking. Things are still seen. They just aren't chased. Fourth, the middle. Half open is the same pair as the rest of this week. Straight and relaxed in the back. Thumbs just touching in the hands. Here, in the eyes: present to the room, not hunting through it. The world isn't shut out, and it isn't grabbed. Half-open eyes keep the sitter in the room, with everyone and everything in it, resting there.
screen: `LIDS HALF DOWN, GAZE ON THE FLOOR.` · `CLOSED: DROWSY OR DREAMING.` · `WIDE: GRABBING AT EVERYTHING.` · `HALF OPEN: IN THE ROOM, AT REST.` · then, large: `SEEN, NOT CHASED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: sit with the eyes half open. Find the posture: straight and relaxed, hands resting, thumbs just touching. Now let the eyelids come halfway down. Let the gaze drop to the floor a little way in front of you, and let it go soft, not fixed on any one spot. If the eyes start to close, lift the lids a little. If they start to hunt around, let them settle back down. Shapes and light can stay at the edges. Nothing needs looking at. The bell holds the time.
The eyes. In zazen, half open, lids lowered, the gaze resting softly on the floor ahead: neither shut out nor grabbing. Today's word.
Your line: half open. Today, once, when a screen has your eyes locked on it, lower your gaze for three breaths, and let the room come back in at the edges. Day one thousand two hundred nine.

howItsDone: In Zen halls, people commonly sit with eyes half open and gaze lowered; in Soto Zen they often sit facing a wall, and in Rinzai Zen facing into the room.

myth: in zazen the eyes are always closed
Dogen's guide says to keep them open; in practice they're half open, gaze lowered.
the gaze in zazen is fixed hard on one spot
it rests softly, unfocused, on the floor ahead.
half-open eyes help keep drowsiness away

fork.setup: you're sitting zazen and your eyes keep sliding shut. you feel sleep coming. what do you do?
options: let them close; it's more peaceful
lift the lids a little and lower the gaze again
open them wide and stare at a spot
fork.reveal: lift the lids back to half open. closed invites drowsiness; wide invites grabbing. half open is the middle.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditating means closing your eyes.
what it means: in zazen the eyes are half open, the gaze resting softly on the floor ahead.
what a scholar hears: Dogen's short guide to sitting tells the sitter to keep the eyes open, not shut.
recall: a householder of Vaishali, not a monk
